title: Expert sparsity, KV-prefetch and batching decisioning - onprem pilot deep dive
summary: Deep technical session with OrchidCloud about optimizing sparse-expert models and runtime knobs for an on-prem pilot. Covered routing cost tradeoffs (tokens, load balancing), ROPE/positional decay effects, practical KV prefetching vs cache warm strategies, and batching/quantization levers. Agreed to run 1-week benchmark using Redwood perf template and to provide SOC2/network docs for pilot approval.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-11-12
Time: 15:00 PST
Duration: ~78 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Ethan (Redwood), Maria (OrchidCloud ML), Tom (OrchidCloud SRE), Li (OrchidCloud Research), Ava (Product)

Auto-generated summary: see separate field - may be rough.

[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone, thanks for joining. uh, quick intro from our side — i'm Jordan, i'll be running the commercial side, priya's gonna drive the technical portion.
[00:08] Maria: thanks, Jordan. quick note, we have low tolerance for cold-start latency spikes, our sla is p95 < 120ms for inference path, okay?
[00:15] Priya: understood. that's tight, especially for MoE routing with large context if you don't prewarm kvcache or do prefix cache. we wanted to align on realistic knobs.
[00:28] Tom: yeah our infra is on-prem, vSphere + private racks, 100Gbps spine but firewalling to the control plane is strict. curious how much inter-node chatter the kv prefetch strategies require.
[00:40] Priya: good call. we'll cover both kv prefill (prefetching key-value shards into local GPU memory) and runtime prefix caching. the trade is warm-up cost vs memory footprint.
[00:52] Li: can you remind me — for Llama vs Mistral vs Qwen are there differences in rope handling that materially change chunking or kv cache behavior? i ask because our models are mixed: some groups use Llama-2-70B variants, others experimenting with Mistral-large 7B kind of setups.
[01:10] Priya: yes, short answer: ROPE/positional embeddings are model-specific and rope scaling (decay, scaling factor) affects long-context KV reuse. with some Llama-family forks, you see more drift -> cache evictions earlier, which makes prefetch less effective. Mistral often has more stable positional handling so you can rely on longer KV reuse windows. Qwen's tokenization and block layout sometimes increases effective sequence length which affects batching.
[01:35] Jordan: maybe to ground this — priya, can you walk the group through a concrete example of routing cost math for a sparse MoE run?
[01:43] Priya: sure. so imagine a 32k-token session, 16 experts, top-k routing with k=2, and each token routes to 2 experts. routing multiplier means multiply per-token expert compute. if baseline dense cost is C per token, MoE effective compute ~ C*(k * expert_compute_fraction + router_overhead). but more importantly you pay memory and cross-node shuffles if experts are sharded across GPUs. so on-prem topology matters.
[02:12] Tom: our racks are 8x A100s per node, all experts pinned to nodes to limit cross-host hops. is that what you recommend?
[02:20] Priya: pinned experts helps but reduces elasticity. there's a continuum: fully pinned -> low network, poor utilization; dynamic placement -> higher shuffles but better utilization. for strict latency SLOs, pinning with local kv prefill is a defensible starting point.
[02:35] Maria: what's the impact on p95 vs p99 for routing shuffles?
[02:39] Priya: typical observation: cross-node shuffles add 5-40ms depending on payload and fabric. p99 can blow up if a node has hotspotting. so routing policies that include token-affinity and knob like token-stickiness or sticky-routing windows substantially reduce tail latency.
[02:57] Li: we have a use-case that streams long dialogues — many repeated prefixes. could continuous batching + kv-prefix caching be enough to meet p95 < 120ms without MoE routing?
[03:09] Priya: possibly. continuous batching that preserves KV caches and microbatching with prefix reuse reduces per-token overhead. the trick is to keep batch sizes small enough to satisfy latency but large enough for throughput. Redwood's runtime supports adaptive batching windows; we can show you live numbers in the pilot.
[03:28] Ava: what about quantization? we're sensitive to accuracy, can't degrade generation quality beyond small delta.
[03:34] Priya: we recommend per-layer mixed-int8 + activation-aware quant profiles for Mistral and Qwen. Llama-family sometimes needs more careful outlier handling. in practice you get 2-3x perf gains with minimal quality loss if you calibrate on representative prompts. we'll provide suggested quant profiles and a validation harness.
[03:58] Jordan: quick interruption — you mentioned token-affinity policies. can you expand?
[04:03] Priya: token-affinity tries to route tokens likely to access same KV shards to same physical expert set over time, reducing cross-host IO. think of it like sticky sessions but at token-embedding level. it adds complexity to router heuristics but can cut shuffle costs significantly.
[04:22] Tom: curious about prefetching — how much RAM/GPU memory overhead are we talking if we prefill 10k tokens worth of KV per GPU?
[04:30] Priya: rough ballpark: for 70B-class models, 10k tokens of KV is hundreds of MBs to several GB depending on kv representation and quant. for quantized kv we can shrink that footprint. warm vs cold numbers vary; i'll include a breakdown in the perf template.
[04:48] Maria: ok can you show an example runtime config that balances p95 with cost?
[04:53] Priya: yes. example: local pinning, kv-prefill to 2k tokens, microbatch size 4, adaptive batching target latency 30ms, quant profile int8-perchannel for FFN, mixed-int8 for kv storage. that setup tends to hold p95 under 100ms on our reference workloads. again, depends on prompt length distribution.
[05:20] Ethan: i'll add that for on-prem we typically advise exploiting GPU-resident cached prefixes and reducing host-device roundtrips by co-locating router and infer workers on same host. avoids PCIe crossings.
[05:32] Li: in our experiments we saw rope scaling causing drift after ~4k tokens, leading to hallucinations in long form. any tips?
[05:40] Priya: two levers: positional re-scaling (a small decay factor) and explicit rolling checkpoints for KV. ROI: rescaling easier but can change semantics; checkpointing lets you preserve earlier states at cost of memory. we also sometimes use relative positional encodings (if model variant supports) to avoid scale drift.
[06:03] Maria: do you have a recommendation for routing params for Llama-2-70b MoE variant?
[06:10] Priya: for that class, start with top-k=1 or 2, enforce max-expert-load threshold at 1.5x average, enable token-stickiness windows of 16-64 tokens. measure expert hotness and adjust.
[06:24] Jordan: switching to benchmarking — we propose Redwood provides a perf harness and cost model: you'll run it in your cluster with our runner, we'll capture p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, GPU utilization, and routing overhead.
[06:36] Tom: firewall / network — what egress/inbound to Redwood control plane is necessary for a private pilot? we need explicit ports and flow docs for our security team.
[06:46] Jordan: we'll send the on-prem networking checklist and SOC2 artifact pack. minimal control plane calls for metrics/rollouts, but inference traffic stays in your VPC, no outbound model traffic.
[07:00] Maria: good. any constraints around model weights staying on-prem?
[07:04] Priya: yes, for private deployment model weights and KV caches remain on your hardware. Redwood control plane only orchestrates; you can opt for air-gapped with manual rollouts for stricter compliance.
[07:16] Li: curious about measuring routing cost per token in the harness — is there a breakdown?
[07:22] Priya: the harness logs: router time, shuffle bytes, expert compute time, kv load misses/hits, and token-level latency. that yields a per-token cost figure so you can tune knobs to meet economics.
[07:35] [08:00] --- (meeting continues with deeper tuning examples) ---
[08:05] Priya: example 2: if you can't prefill due to memory, use progressive prefetch: prefill hot shards first based on token-frequency map and lazy load the rest. this reduces initial warm spike.
[08:20] Tom: ok that aligns with our topology. we do have limited spare GPU memory. progressive approach makes sense.
[08:27] Ava: what about multi-tenant considerations? we might have multiple teams sharing clusters.
[08:31] Priya: prioritize tenant isolation via cgroup-level GPU reservation + per-tenant kv namespaces. routing policies can be tenant-aware to avoid cross-tenant hotspotting.
[08:45] Li: any gotchas with quant + MoE?
[08:48] Priya: yes: quant amplifies router noise if router logits are sensitive to small perturbations; use quantized router with higher-bit precision or run router in fp16 while experts use int8. small hybrid configs often work best.
[09:04] Maria: ok let's recap next steps verbally.
[09:08] Jordan: recap: Redwood sends perf template, cost spreadsheet, SOC2 and on-prem checklist; OrchidCloud to upload prompt corpus and p95 target; schedule benchmark kickoff next week; SE-run bench and share results.
[09:22] Maria: agreed. and please include a sample config for progressive prefetch and token-affinity routing.
[09:29] Priya: will do.
[09:31] Jordan: any final Qs?
[09:33] Tom: none from me.
[09:35] Li: no.
[09:37] Ava: thanks all.
[09:39] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email with links.
